label: HISTORY
title: The Dancing Plague of 1518: The Summer a City Could Not Stop Dancing
description: In July 1518 a woman stepped into a street in Strasbourg and began to dance. She did not stop for days. Within a month, chronicles say, hundreds had joined her, and the city council's cure made everything worse. This is what the records tell us about one of history's strangest outbreaks, and the best explanation we have for it.

sources.title: What Was the Dancing Plague of 1518?, History.com

lines.t: Jack, what is the longest you have ever danced?
A wedding, once. Maybe three hours, with breaks.
In the summer of 1518, in the city of Strasbourg, a woman danced for most of a week. Alone, in the street, without music.
Why?
Nobody knew. She did not seem to know either. And then other people began to join her.
How many?
According to one chronicle, about four hundred within a month. It is known as the dancing plague, and it really is in the city records.
Strasbourg today is in France. In 1518 it was a free city of the Holy Roman Empire, a wealthy trading town on the Rhine.
In the middle of July, a woman the sources call Frau Troffea walked out of her house and started dancing.
Happily?
The accounts suggest the opposite. She did not smile or speak. She danced until she collapsed, slept a little, and got up and danced again.
What did her neighbours think?
At first they watched. Some thought she was doing it to spite her husband. After several days, with her feet bleeding, that idea was dropped.
The authorities had her taken by wagon to a shrine in the hills, dedicated to Saint Vitus. But by then it was too late.
Because others had started.
Within a week, around thirty people were dancing in the streets. The number kept rising.

chapters.heading: A City That Was Already Suffering

lines.t: Before we go on, what was life like in Strasbourg that year?
Terrible. The region had suffered a run of bad harvests. Grain prices were the highest in a generation. Many families had sold their land and animals and were begging.
On top of hunger there was disease. Smallpox, and a frightening new illness, syphilis.
So people were frightened and exhausted.
And they had a ready explanation for misfortune. This was a deeply religious society, and in that region people believed in the anger of Saint Vitus.
What did he have to do with dancing?
It was believed that Saint Vitus could send a curse that forced sinners to dance. Outbreaks of compulsive dancing had been recorded along the Rhine before, most famously in 1374.
So when Frau Troffea began, people recognised it.
They thought they knew exactly what it was. And they feared they might be next.
The city council consulted the physicians. The doctors ruled out the stars and the supernatural.
Sensible so far.
They diagnosed "hot blood". An overheating of the body.
And the treatment?
More dancing. The idea was that the afflicted had to dance the fever out of their systems.
You cannot be serious.

The council cleared two guildhalls and the grain market. They built a wooden stage. They hired musicians with pipes and drums to keep the rhythm, and strong men to hold the dancers upright when they sagged.
In the middle of the city, where everyone could see.
Exactly. Imagine being a frightened citizen who believes this is a curse. You now walk past a public stage where dozens of your neighbours are dancing in agony to official music.
It would spread.
It exploded. This is when the numbers are said to have reached the hundreds.
I have read that people danced themselves to death.
This is where we need to be careful. One later chronicle claims that at the worst point, around fifteen people a day were dying.
That is a huge number.

It is, and the sources written in the city at the time do not mention deaths. So historians disagree. Some dancers very probably did die. Dancing for days in summer heat, with little food or water, would kill some people. But the true number is unknown.
Is there any doubt the event happened at all?
No. It is described in council notes, in sermons, in several chronicles, and by the physician Paracelsus, who visited Strasbourg a few years later and wrote about it.
By August, the council realised its mistake. It reversed everything.
No more stage.
The stage came down. Music and public dancing were banned. Gambling houses were closed. The city ordered penance.
Then the dancers were loaded onto wagons and taken to the shrine of Saint Vitus, in a grotto above the town of Saverne.
What happened there?
Priests said Mass for them. They were given small crosses and pairs of red shoes, which had been sprinkled with holy water. Then they were led around the altar.
And that worked?
According to the chronicles, most of them stopped. By early September the outbreak was over.
So what was actually going on?
One popular theory is ergot. It is a fungus that grows on damp rye and contains chemicals related to LSD. Eat contaminated bread and you can get spasms and hallucinations.
That sounds convincing.
It has a problem. Ergot poisoning also cuts off blood supply to the limbs. Victims can barely walk, let alone dance for days. And it would not explain why everyone reacted in the same way.
Then what?
The explanation most historians accept comes from the medical historian John Waller. He argues it was a mass psychogenic illness.
Meaning it was in their minds.

Meaning real symptoms, produced by extreme stress and shaped by belief. Starving, frightened people who were certain that a saint could curse them with dancing could slip into a kind of trance, and act out exactly what they feared.
And seeing others do it made it more likely.
Which is why the public stage was a disaster, and why a religious ritual ended it. The cure matched the belief.
Has anything like it happened since?
In other forms, yes. In 1962, in what is now Tanzania, an outbreak of uncontrollable laughter began in a girls' school and spread to nearby villages for months.
The detail I cannot get past is the band. Somebody was paid to play for them.
With the best intentions, on medical advice. It is a reminder that a confident wrong diagnosis can be worse than none.
What do you think it was? Poison, belief, or something else?
